rv.q: Rice brings myth, popular culture, circus, comedy and genuine anguish into exhilarating harmony, leaving an understanding of love's inequities that lingers long after the final flourish.
The genre-bending epic romance of Tristan and Yseult will sweep you off your feet.

Such acts of legerdemain are challenging enough; with the medieval legend of Tristan and Yseult , Rice is working without a net. Only a fool would bet against her, however. Aided by writers Carl Grose and Anna Maria Murphy , plus a fine design team and a superhumanly agile cast, Rice puts her singular brand of sorcery to work.

Apparently, a story catches her eye, ear, and imagination at which point all she needs is the inkling that she can do something with it that affords her an entertaining time and, as a result, has the capacity to entertain others, which undeniably this enterprise does.
A sharp and heartfelt core gets buried under a lot of theatrical overaccessorizing.

Instead, Trisan & Yseult is more a cavalcade cabaret riff on the story, featuring some straightforward scenes, but the main attraction here is the spectacle, the song and dance and aerial acrobatics and healthy helpings of comedy. And on that front, this show delivers.
And that sense of limitless playfulness is a source of joy.

cn.t: Emma Rice's inventive adaptation of the medieval legend wins critics over with its genre-blending theatricality, blending myth, music, and comic mayhem into a rip-roaring production anchored by a committed cast.

vr.q: it won me over with its disarmingly irreverent humor, its musicianship, and most of all, its direction
